correctness.rationale: Exact weighted quotient neighbours are \((b+1,c)\) with weight a, \((b-1,c)\) and \((b-1,c+1)\) each with weight b, and \((b+1,c-1)\) with weight c. The first round distinguishes b by degree \(d+b\) and the state \((1,0)\) by adjacency to the marked root. At subsequent rounds, at most one state per b-tail has newly reachable distance \(t+1\) and it has a neighbour in a previously singled reached state; all more-distant states have neighbours exclusively in other merged tails, with multiplicities \(d-b\) and \(2b\) independent of c. The max second-highest state-distance is \(2d-2\), attained at \(b=0\) and witnessed by \((0,d-1)\) and \((0,d)\). Coordinate permutations are all rooted automorphisms: degrees distinguish \(2e_i\) from \(e_i+e_j\) and the distances to \(2e_i\) recover each coordinate. Direct whole-graph computations for \(2\le d\le8\) and independent quotient computations through \(d=60\) in specified samples reproduce every round. Finite computations are corroboration rather than proof of the dimension-uniform theorem.

originality.rationale: Direct claim-level comparison was made with early work on Cartesian-power distinguishing labelings (Albertson 2005; Imrich and Klavžar 2006), general 1-WL and C2 refinement and orbit theory (Arvind et al. 2015; Kiefer et al. 2015), the universal-cover depth bounds of Krebs and Verbitsky (2014), and later extremal round bounds of Kiefer and McKay (2020). Those works do not state or directly imply the explicit per-round tail partition and sharp \(2d-2\) one-corner depth for \(P_3\) Cartesian powers. The distinction is by scientific implications, not absence of a matching phrase. Specialized earlier material might exist, so publication priority is not asserted.

value.rationale: The central object is the \(d\)-dimensional ternary Cartesian grid, a natural product family with exponentially growing order \(3^d\) and many nontrivial rooted automorphisms. The natural invariant is the number of one-dimensional counting refinement rounds and the complete orbit partition after a canonical corner is marked. The theorem gives all intermediate partitions, exact least depth \(2d-2\), an explicit last merged pair, the exact orbit count \(\binom{d+2}{2}\) and every orbit size. The same wavefront induction explains how root information propagates through a high-dimensional symmetric product and provides a reproducible benchmark, not just a finite enumeration, cosmetic reparametrization or trivial degree calculation.
